lesson.title: Where the Curve Begins: Initial Value
lesson.summary: The initial value is the amount present before any growth or decay has happened, the value of y when t equals 0, and it is the coefficient a in y equals a times b raised to the t.
lesson.body:
Every exponential model y equals a times b raised to the t has two important numbers: the factor b, covered in the last two chapters, and the coefficient a, called the initial value. The initial value is simply the amount you start with, the value of y at the very first moment, when t equals 0, before the growth or decay factor has been applied even once.

You can see why algebraically. Substitute t equals 0 into the equation: y equals a times b raised to the 0. Any nonzero number raised to the power 0 equals 1, so b raised to the 0 equals 1, which means y equals a times 1, which is just a. So no matter what the growth or decay factor is, plugging in t equals 0 always hands you the initial value directly.

Here is a worked example. A video is posted online, and the number of views is modeled by V(t) equals 12 times 1.5 raised to the t, where t is the number of days since it was posted. To find the initial value, substitute t equals 0: V(0) equals 12 times 1.5 raised to the 0, which equals 12 times 1, which equals 12. So the video started with 12 views before any of the growth happened. You can check this makes sense with the growth factor of 1.5: one day later, V(1) equals 12 times 1.5, which equals 18, an increase of 6 views, matching a 50 percent increase over 12, exactly what a growth factor of 1.5 predicts.

Sometimes you are not given the equation directly, only a table of values, and you still need to find the initial value. Suppose a table shows days 0, 1, and 2 paired with views 12, 18, and 27. Check that the ratio between consecutive values stays constant: 18 divided by 12 equals 1.5, and 27 divided by 18 equals 1.5, confirming a steady growth factor of 1.5. Once that is confirmed, the initial value is simply the y-value listed at t equals 0, which is 12, with no further computation needed.

A common mistake is to treat the value at t equals 1 as the initial value, or to estimate it from the general starting height of a graph instead of reading the exact value at t equals 0. Getting the initial value exactly right matters a great deal, because it is the very first thing you need to build any exponential model from a word problem, and it plays the same role as the principal P in the compound interest formula covered in the next chapter.
